questions.stem: Where does the verb go in a Japanese sentence?
options: At the end of the sentence
At the start of the sentence
questions.explanation: Japanese puts the verb last: 「わたしはすしを食べます。」 (watashi wa sushi o tabemasu.) is word for word 'I sushi eat'. English puts the verb straight after the subject, which is the habit to break.

questions.stem: Which order describes a normal Japanese sentence?
questions.explanation: Japanese is subject, object, verb: 「ケンさんはテレビを見ます。」 (ken-san wa terebi o mimasu.) is 'Ken TV watches'. English is subject, verb, object, so the verb has to travel to the end.

questions.stem: Which statement about Japanese nouns is true?
options: They are used without words like 'a' or 'the'
They change their ending for the plural
They are either masculine or feminine
They start with a capital letter
questions.explanation: Japanese has no articles, so 「ねこ」 (neko) can be 'a cat' or 'the cat'. There is no gender and no capital letters either — Japanese script has no capitals at all.

questions.stem: How does Japanese usually show that there is more than one of something?
options: It adds -s to the end of the noun, as English does
It adds たち (tachi) to the end of every noun
It changes the final vowel of the noun
The noun does not change; context or a number shows it
questions.explanation: 「本」 (hon) is 'book' or 'books'; a number or the situation makes it clear. たち (tachi) is added to some words for people, as in 「わたしたち」 (watashitachi, 'we'), but not to things.

questions.stem: What is a particle in Japanese?
options: A small word before a noun that means 'the'
An ending added to a verb to show the past
A kanji that shows how a word is read
A small word after a noun that shows its job in the sentence
questions.explanation: Particles such as は (wa), を (o) and に (ni) follow the word they belong to and say what it is doing: topic, object, destination. English uses word order and prepositions for the same job.

questions.stem: In 「学校に行きます。」 (gakkou ni ikimasu.), where does に (ni), meaning 'to', sit?
options: At the very start of the sentence
After the noun it belongs to
Before the noun it belongs to
questions.explanation: English says 'to school', with the little word first. Japanese says 「学校に」 (gakkou ni), 'school to'. Because particles come after the noun, they are sometimes called postpositions.

questions.stem: In 「わたしはりんごを食べます。」 (watashi wa ringo o tabemasu.), what job does を (o) do?
options: It marks the time when the eating happens
It marks the object, the thing being eaten
It marks the topic, the person eating
It marks the place where the eating happens
questions.explanation: を (o) follows the direct object, here 「りんご」 (ringo, apple). The person eating is marked by は (wa), and a place of action would take で (de).

questions.stem: 「すしを食べます。」 (sushi o tabemasu.) has no word for 'I'. Why is it still a complete sentence?
options: The ending ます (masu) means 'I' in Japanese
The particle を (o) stands for 'I' here
すし (sushi) is the subject of the sentence
Japanese often leaves out the subject when it is clear
questions.explanation: Japanese drops the subject whenever the situation makes it obvious, so this means 'I eat sushi' when said about yourself. ます (masu) only makes the verb polite; it does not show who is doing it.

questions.stem: How does a Japanese verb change for 'I', 'you', 'she' or 'they'?
options: It changes only when the subject is plural
It changes only for 'you', to be polite
It does not change; one form serves every person
It takes a different ending for each person
questions.explanation: 「食べます」 (tabemasu) is 'I eat', 'you eat', 'she eats' and 'they eat'. French and German change the verb for each person; Japanese does not, which is one thing that makes it easier.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I watch TV at home'?
options: うちで見ますテレビを。 (uchi de mimasu terebi o.)
うちでテレビを見ます。 (uchi de terebi o mimasu.)
見ますうちでテレビを。 (mimasu uchi de terebi o.)
テレビを見ますうちで。 (terebi o mimasu uchi de.)
questions.explanation: The verb 「見ます」 (mimasu) must come last. The other sentences follow English order and put the verb in the middle or at the front.

questions.stem: Which sentence means the same as 「わたしは土よう日にテニスをします。」 (watashi wa doyoubi ni tenisu o shimasu.)?
options: わたしはテニスに土よう日をします。 (watashi wa tenisu ni doyoubi o shimasu.)
土よう日にわたしはテニスをします。 (doyoubi ni watashi wa tenisu o shimasu.)
わたしは土よう日をテニスにします。 (watashi wa doyoubi o tenisu ni shimasu.)
テニスはわたしを土よう日にします。 (tenisu wa watashi o doyoubi ni shimasu.)
questions.explanation: Because each particle stays with its word, the phrases before the verb can move: 「土よう日に」 (doyoubi ni) still means 'on Saturday' wherever it sits. Swapping the particles, as the other sentences do, changes who does what.

questions.stem: Which particle marks the topic of a sentence?
questions.explanation: は (wa) marks what the sentence is about: 「わたしは学生です。」 (watashi wa gakusei desu.) 'As for me, I am a student.' を (o) marks the object, で (de) a place of action and の (no) belonging.

questions.stem: When は is used as the topic particle, how is it pronounced?
questions.explanation: The topic particle is written は but said wa. In ordinary words は keeps its normal sound ha, as in 「はし」 (hashi). It is one of three particles that are spelt the old way.

questions.stem: When へ is used as a particle meaning 'to', how is it pronounced?
questions.explanation: As a particle, へ is said e: 「日本へ行きます」 (nihon e ikimasu). Inside a word it keeps its normal sound he, as in 「へや」 (heya, room).

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「パン___食べます。」 (pan ___ tabemasu.), 'I eat bread'?
questions.explanation: Bread is the thing being eaten, so it is the object and takes を (o). に (ni) and へ (e) point to a destination, and で (de) marks where an action happens.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「としょかん___本をよみます。」 (toshokan ___ hon o yomimasu.), 'I read books at the library'?
questions.explanation: Reading is an action, and the place where an action happens takes で (de). に (ni) is the tempting mistake: it marks where something exists or where you are going, not where you do something.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「らいねん、日本___行きます。」 (rainen, nihon ___ ikimasu.), 'Next year I am going to Japan'?
questions.explanation: へ (e) marks the direction or destination of movement. で (de) would make Japan the place where an action happens, which does not fit 「行きます」 (ikimasu, go).

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「友だち___こうえんに行きます。」 (tomodachi ___ kouen ni ikimasu.), 'I go to the park with a friend'?
questions.explanation: と (to) means 'with' a person, as well as 'and' between nouns. を (o) would make the friend the object of the going, and の (no) would make it 'my friend's park'.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「わたし___なまえはケンです。」 (watashi ___ namae wa ken desu.), 'My name is Ken'?
questions.explanation: の (no) shows belonging, like 's in English: 「わたしのなまえ」 (watashi no namae) is 'my name'. と (to) would give 'me and name', which makes no sense.

questions.stem: Which particle at the end of a polite sentence turns it into a question?
questions.explanation: Adding か (ka) is all it takes: 「学生です。」 (gakusei desu.) becomes 「学生ですか。」 (gakusei desu ka.) 'Are you a student?' ね (ne) asks for agreement, like 'isn't it', and よ (yo) adds emphasis.

questions.stem: What does も (mo) mean in 「わたしも学生です。」 (watashi mo gakusei desu.)?
questions.explanation: も (mo) replaces は (wa) and means 'too': 'I am a student too.' 'And' between two nouns is と (to), a different particle.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「だれ___来ましたか。」 (dare ___ kimashita ka.), 'Who came?'?
questions.explanation: A question word that is the subject always takes が (ga), never は (wa): 「だれが」 (dare ga), 「何が」 (nani ga). The answer takes が too: 「ケンさんが来ました。」 (ken-san ga kimashita.)

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「わたしはねこ___すきです。」 (watashi wa neko ___ suki desu.), 'I like cats'?
questions.explanation: 「すき」 (suki) is an adjective, not a verb, so the thing liked is marked with が (ga). English 'like' takes an object, which tempts learners towards the object particle, but standard Japanese uses が here.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「わたしはにほんご___わかります。」 (watashi wa nihongo ___ wakarimasu.), 'I understand Japanese'?
questions.explanation: 「わかります」 (wakarimasu) marks the thing understood with が (ga), like 「すき」 (suki) and 「じょうず」 (jouzu). で (de) would mean 'by means of Japanese', which is a different idea.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「へやにねこ___います。」 (heya ni neko ___ imasu.), 'There is a cat in the room'?
questions.explanation: In 'there is' sentences, the thing that exists takes が (ga): place に, thing が, then います or あります. を (o) is for objects of action verbs, and 「います」 (imasu) has no object.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「こうえん___いぬがいます。」 (kouen ___ inu ga imasu.), 'There is a dog in the park'?
questions.explanation: Where something exists takes に (ni), even though English says 'in'. で (de) is for where an action happens: 「こうえんであそびます」 (kouen de asobimasu, play in the park). Existence is not an action, so で is wrong here.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「八時___おきます。」 (hachiji ___ okimasu.), 'I get up at eight o'clock'?
questions.explanation: A clock time takes に (ni): 「八時に」 (hachiji ni), 'at eight'. で (de) is the particle English speakers reach for when they think 'at', but it marks a place of action, not a time.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I'll watch a movie tomorrow'?
options: あしたにえいがを見ます。 (ashita ni eiga o mimasu.)
あしたでえいがを見ます。 (ashita de eiga o mimasu.)
あしたをえいがに見ます。 (ashita o eiga ni mimasu.)
あしたえいがを見ます。 (ashita eiga o mimasu.)
questions.explanation: Time words that are relative to today — 「あした」 (ashita), 「きょう」 (kyou), 「きのう」 (kinou), 「まいにち」 (mainichi) — take no に (ni). Clock times, dates and days of the week do take に.

questions.stem: Which time word is normally followed by に (ni)?
questions.explanation: Days of the week take に (ni): 「日よう日に」 (nichiyoubi ni), 'on Sunday'. 'Today', 'tomorrow' and 'every day' are relative to now and stand on their own without a particle.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「これは先生___本です。」 (kore wa sensei ___ hon desu.), 'This is the teacher's book'?
questions.explanation: の (no) joins two nouns to show belonging: 「先生の本」 (sensei no hon), 'the teacher's book'. The sentence already has its topic marked with は (wa) on 「これ」 (kore).

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「バス___学校に行きます。」 (basu ___ gakkou ni ikimasu.), 'I go to school by bus'?
questions.explanation: で (de) marks the means of doing something, including transport: 「バスで」 (basu de), 'by bus'. と (to) means 'together with', so it would make the bus your companion.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「はし___食べます。」 (hashi ___ tabemasu.), 'I eat with chopsticks'?
questions.explanation: A tool takes で (de): 「はしで」 (hashi de), 'using chopsticks'. English uses 'with' for tools and for people, but Japanese と (to) is only 'with' a person.

questions.stem: In 「友だちとはしで食べます。」 (tomodachi to hashi de tabemasu.), what do と (to) and で (de) each mean?
options: と is 'with' a person; で is 'with' a tool
と is 'with' a tool; で is 'with' a person
と is 'and'; で is 'at' a place
と is 'to' a place; で is 'by' a time
questions.explanation: English uses 'with' twice: 'I eat with a friend with chopsticks'. Japanese separates them, と (to) for company and で (de) for the means.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「ケンさん___まりさんは友だちです。」 (ken-san ___ mari-san wa tomodachi desu.), 'Ken and Mari are friends'?
questions.explanation: と (to) joins two nouns as 'and'. も (mo) means 'too', and の (no) would give 'Ken's Mari', which is not what the English says.

questions.stem: Someone says 「わたしはとうきょうに行きました。」 (watashi wa toukyou ni ikimashita.) Which sentence says that Mari went there too?
options: まりさんもはとうきょうに行きました。 (mari-san mo wa toukyou ni ikimashita.)
まりさんはとうきょうも行きました。 (mari-san wa toukyou mo ikimashita.)
まりさんもとうきょうに行きました。 (mari-san mo toukyou ni ikimashita.)
まりさんはとうきょうにも行きました。 (mari-san wa toukyou ni mo ikimashita.)
questions.explanation: も (mo) attaches to the word it adds to. Here the addition is Mari, so it goes on 「まりさん」 (mari-san) and replaces は (wa). 「とうきょうにも」 (toukyou ni mo) would mean she went to Tokyo as well as somewhere else.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「これはだれ___かさですか。」 (kore wa dare ___ kasa desu ka.), 'Whose umbrella is this?'?
questions.explanation: 「だれの」 (dare no) is 'whose', built the same way as 「先生の」 (sensei no), 'the teacher's'. が (ga) would make 'who' the subject, giving 'who is an umbrella'.

questions.stem: What does adding か (ka) do to 「すしがすきです。」 (sushi ga suki desu.)?
options: It makes it negative: 'I don't like sushi.'
It puts it in the past: 'I liked sushi.'
It makes it stronger: 'I love sushi.'
It turns it into a question: 'Do you like sushi?'
questions.explanation: 「すしがすきですか。」 (sushi ga suki desu ka.) is a question. English changes the word order to ask a question; Japanese keeps the order and adds か (ka).

questions.stem: How does Japanese turn a statement into a question?
options: It adds か (ka) and keeps the word order
It swaps the subject and the verb
It moves the verb to the front
It adds a question word at the start
questions.explanation: 「日本人です。」 (nihonjin desu.) becomes 「日本人ですか。」 (nihonjin desu ka.) Nothing moves. English questions swap words around ('You are' becomes 'Are you'), which Japanese never does.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「わたしは学生___。」 (watashi wa gakusei ___.), 'I am a student'?
questions.explanation: です (desu) links a noun to the topic, like 'am', 'is' and 'are'. います (imasu) and あります mean 'there is' or 'to be somewhere', not 'to be something'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am not a teacher'?
options: わたしは先生ないです。 (watashi wa sensei nai desu.)
わたしは先生じゃです。 (watashi wa sensei ja desu.)
わたしは先生じゃないです。 (watashi wa sensei janai desu.)
わたしは先生ですない。 (watashi wa sensei desu nai.)
questions.explanation: The negative of です (desu) is じゃないです (janai desu). English puts 'not' after 'am', which gives the wrong 「ですない」 (desu nai).

questions.stem: What does 「たなかさんは日本人じゃないです。」 (tanaka-san wa nihonjin janai desu.) mean?
questions.explanation: じゃないです (janai desu) is the present negative of です (desu). The past negative would be じゃなかったです (janakatta desu), and a question would end in か (ka).

questions.stem: Which word completes 「きのうは日よう日___。」 (kinou wa nichiyoubi ___.), 'Yesterday was Sunday'?
questions.explanation: The past of です (desu) is でした (deshita). ました (mashita) is the past ending for verbs, as in 「食べました」 (tabemashita), and cannot follow a noun.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'Yesterday was not a holiday'?
options: きのうはやすみでしたじゃない。 (kinou wa yasumi deshita janai.)
きのうはやすみじゃないです。 (kinou wa yasumi janai desu.)
きのうはやすみじゃなかったです。 (kinou wa yasumi janakatta desu.)
きのうはやすみじゃないでした。 (kinou wa yasumi janai deshita.)
questions.explanation: じゃない (janai) behaves like an い-adjective, so its past is じゃなかった (janakatta) plus です (desu). 「じゃないでした」 (janai deshita) puts the past in the wrong place, a very common slip.

questions.stem: How do you make 「食べます」 (tabemasu) negative?
questions.explanation: ます (masu) becomes ません (masen) for the negative. 「食べました」 (tabemashita) is the past and 「食べましょう」 (tabemashou) is 'let's eat'.

questions.stem: Which form means 'drank'?
options: 飲みませんでした (nomimasen deshita)
questions.explanation: ます (masu) becomes ました (mashita) for the past. 「飲みませんでした」 (nomimasen deshita) is 'did not drink', the past negative.

questions.stem: Which form means 'did not watch'?
questions.explanation: The polite past negative adds でした (deshita) to ません (masen). 「見ません」 (mimasen) is present, 'do not watch' or 'will not watch'.

questions.stem: What does 「行きました」 (ikimashita) mean?
questions.explanation: ました (mashita) is the polite past ending. 'Go' would be 「行きます」 (ikimasu), and 'let's go' is 「行きましょう」 (ikimashou).

questions.stem: What does 「来ませんでした」 (kimasen deshita) mean?
questions.explanation: ませんでした (masen deshita) is the past negative. 'Will not come' is 「来ません」 (kimasen): the ます form has no separate future.

questions.stem: What does 「あしたテニスをします。」 (ashita tenisu o shimasu.) mean?
questions.explanation: The ます form covers both present and future, so with 「あした」 (ashita, tomorrow) it means 'will play'. Japanese has no separate future tense.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「きのう、すしを___。」 (kinou, sushi o ___.), 'I ate sushi yesterday'?
questions.explanation: 「きのう」 (kinou, yesterday) needs the past, ました (mashita). 「食べます」 (tabemasu) is present or future and would clash with 'yesterday'.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「わたしはコーヒーを___。」 (watashi wa koohii o ___.), 'I don't drink coffee'?
options: 飲みませんでした (nomimasen deshita)
questions.explanation: A present negative is ません (masen). Adding でした (deshita) would make it 'didn't drink', about one time in the past rather than a habit.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「せんしゅう、おばあさんのうちに___。」 (senshuu, obaasan no uchi ni ___.), 'Last week I didn't go to my grandmother's house'?
options: 行きませんでした (ikimasen deshita)
questions.explanation: 「せんしゅう」 (senshuu, last week) and 'didn't' together need the past negative, ませんでした (masen deshita). 「行きませんか」 (ikimasen ka) looks negative but is an invitation: 'won't you go?'

questions.stem: What is the ます form of 「かえる」 (kaeru, to go home)?
questions.explanation: 「かえる」 (kaeru) looks like 「たべる」 (taberu), which drops る to give 「たべます」 (tabemasu), but it belongs to the other group: る becomes り. So it is 「かえります」 (kaerimasu), never 「かえます」 (kaemasu).

questions.stem: What does 「行きましょう。」 (ikimashou.) mean?
questions.explanation: ましょう (mashou) means 'let's'. 'I want to go' is 「行きたいです」 (ikitai desu), and 'I won't go' is 「行きません」 (ikimasen).

questions.stem: Which sentence invites a friend to see a movie?
options: えいがを見ましたか。 (eiga o mimashita ka.)
えいがを見たいです。 (eiga o mitai desu.)
えいがを見ませんか。 (eiga o mimasen ka.)
えいがを見ません。 (eiga o mimasen.)
questions.explanation: A negative question, ませんか (masen ka), is the polite way to invite: 'won't you watch?' 「見ましたか」 (mimashita ka) asks whether they saw it, and 「見たいです」 (mitai desu) only says what you want.

questions.stem: A friend says 「あした、こうえんに行きませんか。」 (ashita, kouen ni ikimasen ka.) What are they doing?
options: Saying they won't go to the park tomorrow
Asking if you went to the park yesterday
Telling you not to go to the park
Inviting you to go to the park tomorrow
questions.explanation: ませんか (masen ka) looks negative, but it is an invitation, like 'why don't we go?' Without the か (ka), 「行きません」 (ikimasen) would mean 'I won't go'.

questions.stem: A friend asks 「いっしょに食べませんか。」 (issho ni tabemasen ka.) Which reply accepts?
options: いいえ、食べません。 (iie, tabemasen.)
はい、食べませんでした。 (hai, tabemasen deshita.)
ええ、食べましょう。 (ee, tabemashou.)
questions.explanation: The natural answer to a ませんか (masen ka) invitation is ましょう (mashou), 'yes, let's eat'. Answering はい (hai) and then a negative verb says 'I won't eat', because the negative in the invitation was only politeness.

questions.stem: Which reply politely turns down an invitation for Saturday?
options: 土よう日はいいですね。 (doyoubi wa ii desu ne.)
土よう日にしましょう。 (doyoubi ni shimashou.)
土よう日に行きましょう。 (doyoubi ni ikimashou.)
土よう日はちょっと…。 (doyoubi wa chotto...)
questions.explanation: Trailing off with ちょっと (chotto, 'a little') is the polite Japanese way to say no without saying it. 「いいですね」 (ii desu ne) means 'that sounds good', which accepts.

questions.stem: Which of these is an い-adjective?
questions.explanation: 「大きい」 (ookii, big) is an い-adjective. 「きれい」 (kirei) and 「ゆうめい」 (yuumei) end in い but are な-adjectives, which is why they catch people out.

questions.stem: Which of these is a な-adjective, even though it ends in い?
questions.explanation: 「きれい」 (kirei, pretty, clean) is a な-adjective: 「きれいなへや」 (kirei na heya). Its い is part of the word, not an ending, so it is never changed to くない.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'It is not big'?
options: 大きいじゃないです。 (ookii janai desu.)
questions.explanation: An い-adjective changes its last い to くない (kunai): 「大きい」 (ookii) becomes 「大きくない」 (ookikunai). じゃないです (janai desu) is for nouns and な-adjectives, so putting it after an い-adjective is the most common mistake.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'The park is not quiet'?
options: こうえんはしずかいじゃないです。 (kouen wa shizukai janai desu.)
こうえんはしずかじゃないです。 (kouen wa shizuka janai desu.)
こうえんはしずかくないです。 (kouen wa shizukakunai desu.)
こうえんはしずかないです。 (kouen wa shizukanai desu.)
questions.explanation: 「しずか」 (shizuka) is a な-adjective, so it is negated like a noun with じゃないです (janai desu). The くない (kunai) ending belongs only to い-adjectives.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「きょうのてんきは___。」 (kyou no tenki wa ___.), 'Today's weather is not good'?
options: いいじゃないです (ii janai desu)
questions.explanation: 「いい」 (ii, good) is irregular: it changes from the older form 「よい」 (yoi), so 'not good' is 「よくない」 (yokunai). 「いくない」 (ikunai) follows the rule but is wrong.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'The movie was good'?
options: えいがはいかったです。 (eiga wa ikatta desu.)
えいがはいいでした。 (eiga wa ii deshita.)
えいがはよいでした。 (eiga wa yoi deshita.)
えいがはよかったです。 (eiga wa yokatta desu.)
questions.explanation: The past of an い-adjective is かった (katta), and 「いい」 (ii) uses its older stem: 「よかった」 (yokatta). Adding でした (deshita) to an い-adjective is wrong, because the adjective carries the past itself.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'The test was difficult'?
options: テストはむずかしいでした。 (tesuto wa muzukashii deshita.)
テストはむずかしでした。 (tesuto wa muzukashi deshita.)
テストはむずかしいかったです。 (tesuto wa muzukashiikatta desu.)
テストはむずかしかったです。 (tesuto wa muzukashikatta desu.)
questions.explanation: Drop the final い and add かったです (katta desu). 「むずかしいでした」 (muzukashii deshita) treats the adjective like a noun, which is the usual English-speaker error.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'The room was clean'?
options: へやはきれいかったです。 (heya wa kireikatta desu.)
へやはきれくでした。 (heya wa kireku deshita.)
へやはきれいでした。 (heya wa kirei deshita.)
へやはきれかったです。 (heya wa kirekatta desu.)
questions.explanation: 「きれい」 (kirei) is a な-adjective, so its past is でした (deshita), just like a noun. Treating its final い as an ending gives 「きれかった」 (kirekatta), which is wrong.

questions.stem: How do you say 'a quiet park'?
options: こうえんしずかな (kouen shizuka na)
しずかなこうえん (shizuka na kouen)
しずかいこうえん (shizukai kouen)
questions.explanation: A な-adjective takes な (na) when it sits before a noun. Like English, the adjective comes before the noun, not after it.

questions.stem: How do you say 'an expensive bag'?
options: たかなかばん (taka na kaban)
たかいなかばん (takai na kaban)
questions.explanation: An い-adjective goes straight before the noun with no な (na): 「たかいかばん」 (takai kaban). な belongs only to な-adjectives such as 「しずか」 (shizuka).

questions.stem: Where does an adjective go when it describes a noun directly, as in 'a red car'?
options: After the noun, as in French
At the very end of the sentence
After the particle that follows the noun
Before the noun, as in English
questions.explanation: 「あかいくるま」 (akai kuruma) is 'red car', in the same order as English. An adjective can also end a sentence, as in 「くるまはあかいです。」 (kuruma wa akai desu.), 'The car is red'.

questions.stem: What is unusual about the past tense of an い-adjective, compared with English?
options: It cannot be used in the past at all
It adds ました (mashita) like a verb
The adjective itself changes, as in たかかったです (takakatta desu)
It always adds でした (deshita) after the adjective
questions.explanation: English keeps the adjective the same and changes the verb: 'is expensive', 'was expensive'. A Japanese い-adjective carries the tense itself: 「たかい」 (takai) becomes 「たかかった」 (takakatta). でした (deshita) is for nouns and な-adjectives.

questions.stem: Which word means 'this' for a thing near the speaker?
questions.explanation: The こ- words point near the speaker, そ- near the listener, あ- far from both and ど- ask 'which'. So 「これ」 (kore) is 'this one here'.

questions.stem: A bag is next to the person you are talking to. Which word points to it?
questions.explanation: 「それ」 (sore) is 'that' near the listener. English has only 'this' and 'that'; Japanese splits 'that' into near you, 「それ」, and over there, 「あれ」 (are).

questions.stem: A building is far from both you and your friend. Which word points to it?
questions.explanation: 「あれ」 (are) is 'that one over there', away from both speakers. 「それ」 (sore) is for something near the listener.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「___かばんはだれのですか。」 (___ kaban wa dare no desu ka.), 'Whose is this bag?'?
questions.explanation: When 'this' comes straight before a noun it is 「この」 (kono): 「このかばん」 (kono kaban). 「これ」 (kore) stands alone, and 「ここ」 (koko) means 'here'.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「___は先生のペンです。」 (___ wa sensei no pen desu.), 'That (near you) is the teacher's pen'?
questions.explanation: With no noun after it, 'that' is 「それ」 (sore). 「その」 (sono) must be followed by a noun, as in 「そのペン」 (sono pen), and 「そこ」 (soko) is 'there'.

questions.stem: Which word means 'over there', a place far from both speakers?
questions.explanation: The place words are ここ (koko), そこ (soko), あそこ (asoko) and どこ (doko). 「あれ」 (are) points to a thing and 「あの」 (ano) goes before a noun, not to a place.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「トイレは___ですか。」 (toire wa ___ desu ka.), 'Where is the toilet?'?
questions.explanation: 「どこ」 (doko) asks 'where'. 「どれ」 (dore) is 'which one', 「なに」 (nani) is 'what' and 「だれ」 (dare) is 'who'.

questions.stem: Which word asks 'which one?' when choosing from three or more things?
questions.explanation: 「どれ」 (dore) stands on its own: 「どれですか。」 (dore desu ka.) 「どの」 (dono) also means 'which', but only before a noun.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「___ペンがいいですか。」 (___ pen ga ii desu ka.), 'Which pen would you like?'?
questions.explanation: Before a noun, 'which' is 「どの」 (dono): 「どのペン」 (dono pen). 「どれ」 (dore) replaces the noun, so 「どれペン」 (dore pen) is wrong, in the same way as 「これペン」 (kore pen).

questions.stem: What does 「だれ」 (dare) mean?
questions.explanation: 「だれ」 (dare) is 'who': 「あの人はだれですか。」 (ano hito wa dare desu ka.) 'Who is that person?'

questions.stem: What does 「いつ」 (itsu) mean?
questions.explanation: 「いつ」 (itsu) is 'when': 「たんじょうびはいつですか。」 (tanjoubi wa itsu desu ka.) 'When is your birthday?'

questions.stem: What does 「何ですか。」 (nan desu ka.) mean?
questions.explanation: 「何」 means 'what'. Before です (desu) it is read なん (nan); before を (o) it is なに (nani), as in 「何を食べますか。」 (nani o tabemasu ka.)

questions.stem: What does 「いくらですか。」 (ikura desu ka.) mean?
questions.explanation: 「いくら」 (ikura) asks a price. 'How old are you?' is 「何さいですか。」 (nansai desu ka.) and 'what time' is 「何時」 (nanji).

questions.stem: What does 「何さいですか。」 (nansai desu ka.) mean?
questions.explanation: さい (sai) counts years of age, so 「何さい」 (nansai) is 'how many years old'. Time uses 時 (ji) and people use 人 (nin).

questions.stem: How is 「何」 read in 「何時」?
questions.explanation: 「何」 is read なん before counters such as 時 (ji), さい (sai) and 人 (nin), and before です (desu). It is なに before を (o) and が (ga).

questions.stem: What does 「どんなたべものがすきですか。」 (donna tabemono ga suki desu ka.) mean?
options: When do you eat your food?
Where do you buy your food?
What kind of food do you like?
questions.explanation: 「どんな」 (donna) means 'what kind of' and goes before a noun. The answer names a type of food, for example 「あまいたべもの」 (amai tabemono, sweet food).

questions.stem: Which word completes 「にわにいぬが___。」 (niwa ni inu ga ___.), 'There is a dog in the garden'?
questions.explanation: Living things that move by themselves — people and animals — take 「います」 (imasu). Things and plants take 「あります」 (arimasu).

questions.stem: Which word completes 「つくえの上に本が___。」 (tsukue no ue ni hon ga ___.), 'There is a book on the desk'?
questions.explanation: A book is an object, so it takes 「あります」 (arimasu). 「います」 (imasu) is only for people and animals.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have an older sister'?
options: あねをいます。 (ane o imasu.)
あねがいます。 (ane ga imasu.)
あねがあります。 (ane ga arimasu.)
questions.explanation: Japanese says 'there is an older sister', and a person takes 「います」 (imasu). English 'have' tempts learners towards を (o), but 「います」 has no object.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have a test tomorrow'?
options: あしたテストをあります。 (ashita tesuto o arimasu.)
あしたテストでいます。 (ashita tesuto de imasu.)
あしたテストがあります。 (ashita tesuto ga arimasu.)
あしたテストがいます。 (ashita tesuto ga imasu.)
questions.explanation: Events such as tests, parties and classes take 「あります」 (arimasu), the verb for things. The test is what exists, so it takes が (ga), not を (o).

questions.stem: Why do you say 「先生がいます」 (sensei ga imasu) but 「いすがあります」 (isu ga arimasu)?
options: います is for people and animals; あります is for things
います is for things; あります is for people and animals
います is for one; あります is for more than one
います is present; あります is past
questions.explanation: Japanese has two verbs for 'there is'. A teacher is a person, so 「います」 (imasu); a chair is a thing, so 「あります」 (arimasu).

questions.stem: Someone asks 「ペットがいますか。」 (petto ga imasu ka.) Which reply says 'No, I don't have one'?
options: いいえ、ありません。 (iie, arimasen.)
いいえ、いませんでした。 (iie, imasen deshita.)
いいえ、じゃないです。 (iie, janai desu.)
questions.explanation: A pet is an animal, so the answer keeps the verb 「います」 (imasu) and makes it negative: 「いません」 (imasen). 「いませんでした」 (imasen deshita) would mean you had none in the past.

questions.stem: What does 「日本に行きたいです。」 (nihon ni ikitai desu.) mean?
options: I want to go to Japan.
questions.explanation: たいです (tai desu) replaces ます (masu) to mean 'want to': 「行きます」 (ikimasu) becomes 「行きたいです」 (ikitai desu). 'Let's go' would be 「行きましょう」 (ikimashou).

questions.stem: Which form completes 「ラーメンを___。」 (raamen o ___.), 'I want to eat ramen'?
questions.explanation: Take the ます form, remove ます (masu) and add たい (tai): 「食べます」 (tabemasu) becomes 「食べたいです」 (tabetai desu). The たい goes in place of ます, never after it.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「きょうは学校に___。」 (kyou wa gakkou ni ___.), 'I don't want to go to school today'?
options: 行きたいないです (ikitainai desu)
行きたくないです (ikitakunai desu)
行きたいじゃないです (ikitai janai desu)
questions.explanation: A たい form behaves like an い-adjective, so its negative is たくない (takunai). じゃないです (janai desu) belongs to nouns and な-adjectives.

questions.stem: What does 「オーストラリア人」 (oosutorariajin) mean?
questions.explanation: Adding 人 (jin) to a country makes a person from it: 「日本人」 (nihonjin) is a Japanese person. The country alone is 「オーストラリア」 (oosutoraria).

questions.stem: What does 「十二さいです。」 (juunisai desu.) mean?
questions.explanation: さい (sai) counts years of age. Twelve o'clock is 「十二時」 (juuniji), and twelve people is 「十二人」 (juuninin).

questions.stem: What does 「三時です。」 (sanji desu.) mean?
questions.explanation: 時 (ji) after a number gives the hour. Minutes use 分 (fun or pun), as in 「三分」 (sanpun).

questions.stem: What does 「三時半」 (sanji han) mean?
questions.explanation: 半 (han) means 'half', and it adds half an hour to the time before it: 3:30. It never means half an hour before the hour.

questions.stem: How is 「四時」 (4 o'clock) read?
questions.explanation: Four is usually よん, but with 時 it shortens to よじ. This is one of the readings that has to be learnt on its own.

questions.stem: How is 「九時」 (9 o'clock) read?
questions.explanation: Nine is usually きゅう, but the hour is always くじ. Nine minutes, by contrast, is きゅうふん, so each counter has to be learnt with its number.

questions.stem: How is 「四人」 read in 「かぞくは四人です。」, 'There are four people in my family'?
questions.explanation: Four people is よにん, without the ん of よん. One and two people are irregular too: ひとり and ふたり.

questions.stem: How do you say 'two people' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: One and two people have their own words: ひとり (hitori) and ふたり (futari). From three on, the counter is 人 (nin): さんにん (sannin), よにん (yonin).

questions.stem: How do you say 'three people' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: From three people on, the number is followed by にん (nin): さんにん (sannin). Only one and two people, ひとり (hitori) and ふたり (futari), end in り (ri).

questions.stem: How is 「一さい」 (one year old) read?
questions.explanation: いち shortens to いっ before さ, doubling the s sound: いっさい. The same shortening happens with other counters, as in 一本, いっぽん.

questions.stem: Which question asks how many people are in someone's family?
options: かぞくは何時ですか。 (kazoku wa nanji desu ka.)
かぞくはいくらですか。 (kazoku wa ikura desu ka.)
かぞくは何人ですか。 (kazoku wa nannin desu ka.)
かぞくは何さいですか。 (kazoku wa nansai desu ka.)
questions.explanation: 人 (nin) counts people, so 「何人」 (nannin) is 'how many people'. The answer uses the same counter: 「四人です。」 (yonin desu.)

questions.stem: 「ねこがすきです。」 (neko ga suki desu.) means 'I like cats'. Which parts of the English have nothing matching them in the Japanese?
options: The word 'I' and the plural -s on 'cats'
questions.explanation: The subject is left out because it is obvious, and 「ねこ」 (neko) has no plural form. 'Like' is there, as 「すき」 (suki), with が (ga) marking what is liked.

questions.stem: English says 'I went to school with a friend'. In what order does 「友だちと学校に行きました。」 (tomodachi to gakkou ni ikimashita.) give the ideas?
questions.explanation: Each particle follows its noun, so 'with a friend' becomes 「友だちと」 (tomodachi to), 'friend with', and the verb comes last. English puts the verb second and the prepositions in front of their nouns.

questions.stem: Why can the phrases before the verb move around in a Japanese sentence without changing who does what?
options: The first word is always the subject
Japanese sentences have no subject or object
Each particle stays with its noun and shows its role
The verb changes its ending to show the subject
questions.explanation: In 「ケンさんがまりさんを見ました。」 (ken-san ga mari-san o mimashita.) the が (ga) and を (o) show who saw whom, whatever the order. In English, swapping 'Ken saw Mari' to 'Mari saw Ken' changes the meaning, because English relies on word order.

questions.stem: In 「ケンさんの本」 (ken-san no hon), 'Ken's book', which part of the English does の (no) match?
questions.explanation: の (no) shows belonging, so 「わたしの」 (watashi no) is 'my' and 「ケンさんの」 (ken-san no) is 'Ken's'. 'And' between nouns is と (to), and 'is' is です (desu).

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I go to school at eight o'clock'?
options: 八時に学校に行きます。 (hachiji ni gakkou ni ikimasu.)
八時で学校に行きます。 (hachiji de gakkou ni ikimasu.)
八時に学校で行きます。 (hachiji ni gakkou de ikimasu.)
行きます八時に学校に。 (ikimasu hachiji ni gakkou ni.)
questions.explanation: The time and the destination both take に (ni), and the verb comes last. で (de) belongs to neither a clock time nor a destination.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「きのう、テレビを___。」 (kinou, terebi o ___.), 'I didn't watch TV yesterday'?
questions.explanation: 'Didn't' about yesterday needs the past negative, ませんでした (masen deshita). 「見ません」 (mimasen) is present or future: 'I don't watch' or 'I won't watch'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'There are two cats under the table'?
options: テーブルの下にねこが二ひきあります。 (teeburu no shita ni neko ga nihiki arimasu.)
テーブルの下にねこを二ひきいます。 (teeburu no shita ni neko o nihiki imasu.)
テーブルの下にねこが二ひきいます。 (teeburu no shita ni neko ga nihiki imasu.)
テーブルの下でねこが二ひきいます。 (teeburu no shita de neko ga nihiki imasu.)
questions.explanation: Existence takes に (ni) for the place, が (ga) for what exists and 「います」 (imasu) for animals. Each wrong sentence breaks one of those three choices.

questions.stem: Which word means 'here'?
questions.explanation: 「ここ」 (koko) is the place word for 'here'. 「これ」 (kore) is 'this thing', 「この」 (kono) is 'this' before a noun, and 「そこ」 (soko) is 'there'.
